country.lede: What is the central bank that sets Germany's interest rate dealing with right now, and what will it most likely do at its next meeting? Germany does not set its own rate: the European Central Bank (ECB) sets one rate for all 21 countries that use the euro. This page explains it from the very beginning, in everyday language, one step at a time. You do not need any background in money or economics.

verdict.headline: HOLD
verdict.sub: Keep the interest rate where it is, at 2.50%. This is a close call. A third rise this year is a very real possibility.
verdict.confidence_note: “Low” means our answer could flip. Euro-area prices jumped to 3.8% in September. The final September price report on Friday, October 16, and the path of oil prices over the next two weeks could be enough to change our answer.
verdict.short_version: The ECB has raised its rate twice this year, both times at meetings where it also published new forecasts (June and September). October has no new forecasts; December does. Prices jumped again in September, so a rise is close, but we think the ECB will more likely wait until December than act in October.
verdict.card_why: Euro-area inflation jumped to 3.8%, but the ECB has moved only at meetings with new forecasts, and those come in December.

why_steps.title: Germany shares one central bank, one goal and one main tool with 20 other countries
why_steps.html: Germany uses the euro, so its main interest rate is not set in Berlin or by the Bundesbank alone. It is set by the European Central Bank for the whole euro area: 21 countries, from Germany and France to Croatia and Bulgaria. The Bundesbank President, Joachim Nagel, sits on the ECB's decision-making Governing Council alongside the other national central bank heads and the six-person ECB Executive Board. As Nagel put it himself: “monetary policy is set uniformly for the entire euro area.” The ECB's main job is keeping prices steady. Its target is that prices across the whole euro area rise by about 2% a year, measured by a gauge called HICP (the Harmonised Index of Consumer Prices, compiled by Eurostat, the EU's statistics office). That means the ECB looks at the euro-area average, not at Germany alone. On this page we show both: the euro-area numbers the ECB targets, and the German numbers that matter to people living in Germany. Its main tool is its interest rate. Today the headline rate is the deposit facility rate, the interest banks get for parking money overnight at the central bank. Think of it like the pedals of a car. Raising the rate is pressing the brake: loans get more expensive, so people and companies borrow and spend less, and prices cool down. Cutting the rate is pressing the gas. Holding means keeping your foot where it is.

why_steps.title: Right now, prices are the bigger problem
why_steps.html: Prices across the euro area were 3.8% higher in September than a year earlier, according to Eurostat's first (“flash”) estimate. In simple terms: a basket of everyday things that cost €100 a year ago now costs about €103.80. The goal would be about €102. In Germany the rise was 3.3%, the highest since December 2023, according to the Federal Statistical Office (Destatis). The main cause is energy. A war in the Middle East this year pushed up oil and gas prices. Across the euro area, energy prices were up 18.8% in a year. In Germany, heating oil cost 74.9% more than a year earlier and fuel at the pump 37.1% more. Brent crude oil, the European benchmark, was about $125 a barrel on October 6. Energy matters for everything, because trucks carry food to shops, factories run machines, and homes need heating, so higher energy costs slowly spread into the price of almost everything. The good news is that prices without energy and food (“core” inflation) are much calmer: 2.5% in the euro area and 2.4% in Germany. The ECB's big worry is that expensive energy starts to leak into everything else, through higher shop prices and higher wage demands.

why_steps.title: So in June and September the ECB pressed the brake
why_steps.html: On June 11 the ECB raised its rate from 2.00% to 2.25%. On September 10, at a meeting held in Berlin, it raised it again to 2.50% (in force from September 16). President Lagarde called the September move “a unanimous decision”. ECB staff forecasts published that day expect euro-area prices to rise 3.0% on average in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028, and the economy to grow 0.9% this year. But the ECB does not publish a promise about its next step. It says it is “not pre-committing to a particular rate path”, and Lagarde added: “We are not taking a view as to which direction we go at our next meeting.” Only two meetings remain this year: October 29 and December 17. Financial markets at the time of the September meeting expected more rises over the next year, so the question is mainly when the next one comes.

why_steps.title: Reasons the ECB might wait until December
why_steps.html:
• The ECB has been moving at “forecast” meetings. Both rises this year (June and September) came at meetings where staff also published new projections. Vice-President Boris Vujčić said it plainly: “We had two rate increases at projection meetings.” October has no new projections. December does.
  • The market already pressed the brake a little. The 10-year German government bond rate rose from 3.39% (Sep 8) to 3.47% (Oct 8). Chief Economist Philip Lane said a rise in long-term rates “slows down the European economy and, on its own, reduces the inflation rate.”
  • No clear signs yet of prices spreading into wages. The ECB's September meeting notes said “So far, indirect effects remained contained, with no material signs of second-round effects.” Bundesbank President Nagel said there are “so far no clear signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting.”
  • Germany's economy is fragile. German employment was 235,000 lower in August than a year earlier, and registered unemployment is near 3 million. The head of the ifo Institute said the September rise “comes at an inopportune time for Germany”.
  • The brake takes time to work. The last rise only took effect on September 16. A rate change takes many months to fully reach the economy.

why_steps.title: Reasons the ECB might raise in October anyway
why_steps.html:
• Prices jumped again. Euro-area inflation leapt from 3.2% in August to 3.8% in September, well above the 3.0% average the ECB's own staff forecast for this year.
  • Energy is worse than the ECB assumed. Lane said in early October that “energy prices are higher than we expected in our baseline.” Brent oil touched $135.51 on October 2.
  • Businesses are passing costs on. The share of German firms planning to raise prices rose in September, and ifo said “This indicates that the higher energy prices are increasingly being passed on to sales prices.”
  • A weaker euro makes imports dearer. One euro bought $1.1539 on September 15 but only $1.1188 on October 13. Oil is priced in dollars, so a weaker euro makes energy even more expensive in Europe.
  • Some officials already fear the worse case. The September meeting notes record that “the view was also held that the adverse scenario was more likely than the baseline.” Nagel said the uncertainty “calls for flexibility, not inaction.”

why_steps.title: Weighing both sides

left: Energy above the ECB's own assumption

why_steps.html: Both sides are strong. What tips us toward Hold is that the ECB has twice chosen to act at forecast meetings, it keeps saying it decides “meeting by meeting” with no promise, and December gives it a full new set of forecasts plus more data at little cost. What keeps Raise close is the September jump to 3.8% and an oil price that is still climbing. That is why we say about 60% Hold and 37% Raise, not something more lopsided. A cut (about 3%) would need a sudden financial shock.

why_steps.title: The one thing to watch: Friday's final price report
why_steps.html: On Friday, October 16, Eurostat publishes the final September inflation figures for the euro area, with full detail by country and category. If core inflation (without energy, food, alcohol and tobacco) is revised up to 2.6% or more, or services inflation reaches 3.4% or more, that would show energy is spreading into everything else and we would likely switch our main call to Raise. If core stays at 2.5% or lower and Brent oil eases back below about $110 a barrel before the meeting, we would be more confident in Hold. These thresholds are Quant Flow's own judgement, not ECB rules.

timeline.title: A calm period: the rate stayed at 2.00%
timeline.what: The ECB held its rate at 2.00% at its meetings on September 11, October 30 and December 18, 2025. It had already cut from 4% to 2% over the previous year and a half; the last cut took effect in June 2025.
timeline.why: Inflation looked under control. In December the ECB said it held “because inflation is on track to settle around our 2% target.”
timeline.people: Loan and savings rates in Germany stayed fairly stable. Borrowing was much cheaper than in 2023–24.
timeline.because: the ECB entered 2026 with its foot off both pedals, expecting inflation to stay near 2%.

timeline.title: Still holding: “inflation stabilising where we want it to be”
timeline.what: The ECB held at 2.00%. Its plain-language explainer said: “We did this because we see inflation stabilising where we want it to be: 2%.” Euro-area inflation was 1.7% in January.
timeline.why: Energy had been getting cheaper and wage growth was slowing, so there was no reason to move.
timeline.people: Nothing much changed. At this point nobody was talking about raising rates.
timeline.because: the ECB was sitting still when a new problem arrived: war in the Middle East.

timeline.title: An energy shock: war in the Middle East
timeline.what: The ECB held at 2.00% but warned: “The war in the Middle East has made the outlook significantly more uncertain.” Staff raised their 2026 inflation forecast to 2.6% (from data collected up to March 11). The ECB said it would “stand ready to adjust all of our instruments within our mandate.”
timeline.why: When oil and gas get expensive, it does not just raise fuel prices. It raises the cost of heating, shipping, farming and making things, so prices across the economy creep up.
timeline.people: Filling the car and heating the home started to get noticeably more expensive. Inflation had been just 1.9% in February.
timeline.because: the ECB began watching closely whether expensive energy would spread into other prices.

timeline.title: Holding again, but inflation is rising
timeline.what: The ECB held at 2.00%. Its explainer said: “Inflation has gone up, and we expect it to stay higher for a while.” Euro-area inflation reached 3.0% in April.
timeline.why: Energy prices kept climbing. The ECB wanted to see how long the war would last before acting.
timeline.people: Household budgets were squeezed by energy bills. The talk in markets shifted from “no change” to “possible rate rises”.
timeline.because: with inflation still rising in May, the ECB decided that waiting was no longer enough.

timeline.title: First rise: the rate goes to 2.25%
timeline.what: The ECB raised its rate by 0.25 points to 2.25% (in force June 17). Lagarde called it “a unanimous decision, without reservation.” May inflation was 3.2%, with services at 3.5%.
timeline.why: The ECB's explainer said: “We are doing this because the war in the Middle East is driving up prices.” Staff expected 3.0% inflation in 2026.
timeline.people: Variable-rate loans and new credit got slightly dearer. Savings accounts started to pay a little more.
timeline.because: the ECB then paused to see whether one rise was enough.

timeline.title: A pause: inflation eases for a month
timeline.what: The ECB held at 2.25%. June inflation had dipped to 2.8%. Lagarde said the decision was unanimous, though some governors asked whether a rise should be considered; the Council felt “positioned adequately to wait.” She added: “The burden of proof is on data, as simple as that.”
timeline.why: One calmer month gave the ECB room to wait. But Lagarde warned that oil and gas were rising again as she spoke.
timeline.people: Loan and savings rates stayed about the same over the summer.
timeline.because: everyone watched the August data to see whether prices would calm down on their own. They did not.

timeline.title: Prices hot again, the economy holding up
timeline.what: Euro-area inflation rose to 3.2% in August, with energy up 14.3%. The euro-area economy grew 0.6% in spring (April–June); Germany grew 0.3%. The ifo business climate in Germany rose for a second month, to 89.9 in September.
timeline.people: Germans paid much more for heating oil and fuel, while their jobs market was slowly getting weaker.
timeline.because: the ECB concluded that it needed to press the brake again.

timeline.title: Second rise: the rate goes to 2.50%
timeline.what: Meeting in Berlin, the ECB raised by 0.25 points to 2.50% (in force September 16). Lagarde called it “a unanimous decision”. Staff now expect inflation of 3.0% in 2026, 2.5% in 2027 and 2.1% in 2028.
timeline.people: Rates on new loans and variable mortgages edged up. Savings and overnight deposits started paying slightly more.
timeline.because: attention turned to whether September's prices would confirm or ease the pressure.

timeline.title: September prices jump; German jobs market sluggish
timeline.what: Euro-area inflation jumped to 3.8% (flash), with energy up 18.8% and core at 2.5%. German inflation rose to 3.3%; heating oil was up 74.9% in a year. Brent oil hit $135.51 on October 2. In Germany, 2.994 million people were registered unemployed (6.4%). The German government cut fuel tax by 17 cents a litre from October 1.
timeline.people: Heating and driving got much more expensive just before winter. The fuel tax cut softens the pain at the pump, but ifo found stations passed on only part of it at first.
timeline.because: the case for another rise grew, and everyone listened closely to what ECB officials would say.

timeline.title: What ECB officials said after the rise
timeline.because: our reading is “another rise is possible, but more likely in December”, which is why our main call is Hold, with Raise close behind.

choices.title: Hold: keep the rate at 2.50%
choices.meaning: the ECB keeps its foot where it is on the brake. It would likely repeat that it stands ready to act, so a hold here would be a “not yet”, not an “all clear”.
for: Forecast meetings. Both rises this year came at meetings with new staff projections. October has none; December does.
The market did some of the work. The 10-year Bund rate rose to 3.47%, which makes mortgages and business loans dearer anyway.
No wage spiral yet. The ECB and Nagel both say there are no clear signs that energy costs are feeding into wages.
Germany is fragile. Employment is falling and unemployment is near 3 million.
The September rise needs time to work. It took effect only six weeks before the meeting.
against: Inflation jumped. 3.8% in September is far above the 2% goal and above the ECB's own 3.0% forecast for the year.
Energy is worse than assumed. Lane said so himself in early October.
The euro is weaker, which makes imported energy dearer still.
A hot final price report on October 16 could make waiting feel too risky.
choices.everyday: loan and savings rates in Germany would stay roughly where they are for now. Attention would then shift to December, when new forecasts arrive.

choices.title: Raise: up 0.25 points, to 2.75%
choices.meaning: the ECB presses the brake harder, for the third time this year and the second meeting in a row, to show it will not let energy prices push up everything else.
for: Prices are moving the wrong way. Euro-area inflation went from 2.8% in June to 3.8% in September.
Energy is still climbing. Brent oil was about $125 a barrel on October 6, and the ECB says gas is especially vulnerable this winter.
Firms are passing costs on. ifo's survey shows more German firms planning price rises.
Some officials fear the worse case. Meeting notes record a view that the adverse scenario was more likely than the baseline.
Lagarde's words. She said in September “we are obliged to react” to a longer-lasting shock.
against: No new forecasts in October. The ECB has preferred to move when it can explain itself with fresh projections.
Core inflation is still moderate at 2.5% in the euro area and 2.4% in Germany.
Germany's economy is weak, and a third rise in five months would hit it hard.
choices.everyday: variable loans and new mortgages would get a little dearer, and savings accounts would pay a bit more. The euro might firm slightly, which would make fuel and imports a little cheaper.

choices.title: Cut: lower the rate
choices.meaning: the ECB would switch from the brake to the gas, reversing its September decision.
for: Only in an emergency: for example a sudden market crash, a serious problem at a big bank, or disorderly turmoil in government bond markets before the meeting.
Even then, the ECB would more likely hold, or use its other tools, than cut straight away.
against: The ECB just raised. Cutting six weeks later would confuse people and damage its credibility.
Nobody is asking for it. In the speeches and interviews we read since September, no ECB official argued for a cut.
Inflation is rising. Cutting would add fuel to it.
choices.everyday: loans would get slightly cheaper, but the surprise itself would likely signal that something had gone badly wrong.

change.lead: Our 60% / 37% / 3% guess is based on what we know today. New information arrives almost every day. Some of it can move our view a lot. Here is what we are watching, and why each item matters.
change.intro: The ECB can only react to information it has already seen. A report released before October 29 can change the October decision. A report released after it can only shape what happens in December. That is why the reports in the first part of the table matter most right now. Where we could not confirm an official release date, we say so.

euro_area_inflation_hicp.why: The most important report before the meeting. It shows whether price pressure is spreading beyond energy.
euro_area_inflation_hicp.trigger: Core revised to 2.6% or more, or services 3.4% or more → Raise becomes our top pick. Core at 2.5% or less → more confident in Hold.

brent_oil_price.why: Energy is the main driver of today's inflation, and the ECB says energy is already above its assumptions.
brent_oil_price.trigger: Brent staying above about $130 → leans Raise. Falling back below about $110 → leans Hold.

ifo_business_climate.why: The fastest read on whether German firms are coping with high energy costs and higher rates.
ifo_business_climate.trigger: A sharp fall → leans Hold. A third rise in a row → small push toward Raise.

german_consumer_prices_cpi_oct.why: It will show the first effect of the 17-cent fuel tax cut from October 1, which should lower German prices at the pump. We could not confirm whether it is published before or after the decision.
german_consumer_prices_cpi_oct.trigger: If out before the decision: a big drop from 3.3% (thanks to the fuel tax cut) would make waiting easier.

german_labour_market.why: Too late for October, but shows whether Germany's jobs market is weakening further.

euro_area_and_german_gdp_q3_fi.why: Shows whether the economy can handle more rate rises.

euro_area_inflation_hicp_octob.why: Key input for December. Will show whether September's jump was a peak.

german_labour_market_2.why: Another check on Germany's jobs market before December.

change.other_title: Other things that could move our view
other: Oil, gas and the Middle East. Energy is the main driver of today's inflation. Nagel warned that gas prices are especially vulnerable because storage levels are low. A new jump in oil or gas would make a rise more likely; a big drop would make waiting easier.
The euro. The euro fell from $1.1539 (Sep 15) to $1.1188 (Oct 13). A further slide makes imported energy dearer and adds to the case for a rise.
Bond market rates. One reason for Hold is that German long-term rates already rose. If they fall back sharply, that reason weakens.

Final words from ECB officials. ECB policymakers normally stop commenting on policy shortly before each meeting (a “quiet period”). Anything Lagarde, Lane, Schnabel or Nagel say before then is the last direct hint we get. We did not confirm the exact start date.

A financial shock. Turmoil in euro-area government bond markets or trouble at a big bank would almost certainly push the ECB to hold. The ECB says its Transmission Protection Instrument is available for disorderly market dynamics.

report_card.one: Things cost 3.8% more than a year ago across the euro area (3.3% in Germany), far above the 2% goal.
report_card.look: Euro-area HICP inflation (3.8%, the ECB's target measure), core inflation without energy and food (2.5%), services (3.2%), and German consumer prices (3.3%).
report_card.why: The ECB's target measure is almost twice the goal and rose sharply in September. Energy is up 18.8% in a year. German producer prices are up 4.6% and import prices 8.3%, which can reach shop shelves later. The ECB says the risks to inflation are “to the upside”.
report_card.change: Energy prices falling back, and several months of core inflation at or below 2.5% with no pick-up in wages.
report_card.matters: This is the reason the ECB is raising rates at all. As long as this stays red, the ECB leans toward the brake.

report_card.one: Euro-area unemployment is low, but Germany's jobs market is slowly weakening.
report_card.look: Euro-area unemployment (Eurostat), German registered unemployment (Bundesagentur für Arbeit), German employment (Destatis), short-time work and vacancies.
report_card.why: Good news: euro-area unemployment is 6.4%, close to historic lows, and German short-time work is falling. Bad news: Germany has 2.994 million registered unemployed (40,000 more than a year earlier), and 235,000 fewer people in work than a year ago. The head of Germany's employment agency said the autumn pick-up started “schwunglos” (without momentum).
report_card.change: Rising unemployment across the euro area → red. German hiring picking up → green.
report_card.matters: The ECB's target is prices, but a weak jobs market, especially in its biggest economy, makes another rise riskier.

report_card.one: The euro area is growing; Germany is growing slowly.
report_card.look: GDP (the total value of everything produced) for the euro area and Germany, the ifo business climate, German industrial production and orders.
report_card.why: The euro area grew 0.6% in spring (Q2), Germany only 0.3%. The ifo index rose to 89.9 in September and production jumped 2.0% in August. But German orders fell 10.6% in August (mostly after a one-off surge in big orders for ships, trains and planes), consumers are barely spending more (+0.1%), and the Bundesbank estimates Germany's underlying growth potential at just 0.4%.
report_card.change: A weak official summer GDP number or a falling ifo index → red. Strong growth across the euro area → green.
report_card.matters: The ECB staff expect 0.9% growth this year. A resilient economy gives the ECB room to raise; a weak Germany argues for caution.

report_card.one: Borrowing costs are rising and the euro is weakening, but long-term inflation expectations are calm.
report_card.look: German government bond rates (Bund yields), the euro–dollar exchange rate, and long-term inflation expectations reported by the ECB.
report_card.why: Worrying: the 10-year Bund rate rose from 3.39% to 3.47% in a month and the 30-year rate is 3.84%, making mortgages dearer. The euro fell about 3% against the dollar, making oil dearer. Reassuring: the ECB says most measures of longer-term inflation expectations “continued to stand at around 2%”, and Nagel says market and expert expectations remain consistent with the 2% target.
report_card.change: Disorderly bond-market moves or a sharp rise in long-term inflation expectations → red. Bond rates and the euro stabilising → green.
report_card.matters: Higher market rates already slow the economy, one reason the ECB may wait. Calm long-term expectations mean the ECB does not need to panic. A weak euro pushes the other way.

euro_area_inflation_hicp_the_ecb_s_tar.what: Eurostat checks the prices of thousands of everyday things across all 21 euro countries and compares them with a year ago. A 3.8% rise means a €100 shopping basket now costs about €103.80.
euro_area_inflation_hicp_the_ecb_s_tar.why: this is the number the ECB's 2% goal is based on. It jumped 0.6 points in one month. It is a first estimate; the final figure comes on October 16, before the meeting.

euro_area_core_inflation_without_energ.what: the same price check with the jumpiest items removed, to show the slower trend underneath.
euro_area_core_inflation_without_energ.why: this tells the ECB whether energy is leaking into everything else. It is only a little above 2% and ticked up just 0.1 point. The number to watch on October 16.

euro_area_energy_prices.what: the price of fuel, heating oil, electricity and gas for households across the euro area.
euro_area_energy_prices.why: this is the main reason inflation is high. Energy feeds into almost every other price over time.

euro_area_services_prices.what: prices for things like restaurants, holidays, rents, repairs and insurance.
euro_area_services_prices.why: services are mostly labour, so they show whether wages and costs are pushing prices up. A steady climb here would worry the ECB more than energy alone.

german_consumer_prices_cpi.what: Germany's own price index. The EU-standard version for Germany (HICP) was also +3.3%.
german_consumer_prices_cpi.why: it shows what people in Germany are feeling. Germany is below the euro-area average (3.8%), which is one reason German voices like ifo's Clemens Fuest see rate rises as badly timed for Germany.

german_core_inflation_without_food_and.what: German prices with food and energy removed.
german_core_inflation_without_food_and.why: it has not moved for three months, a sign that in Germany energy has not (yet) spread widely. German services prices were up 2.7%.

german_energy_prices.what: household energy in Germany. Heating oil was up 74.9% and motor fuels 37.1%, while electricity (−5.5%) and natural gas (−2.8%) were cheaper than a year ago.
german_energy_prices.why: the shock is concentrated in oil products. A fuel tax cut of 17 cents a litre from October 1 should pull German fuel prices down in October.

german_producer_prices_industry.what: prices German factories and energy suppliers charge their business customers. Without energy they were up 3.1%.
german_producer_prices_industry.why: businesses usually pass higher costs on to customers a few months later. It is an early warning for shop prices.

german_import_prices.what: the price of goods Germany buys from abroad. Imported crude oil was up 32.0% and natural gas 41.9%.
german_import_prices.why: Germany imports almost all its oil and gas, so this is how the Middle East shock enters the German economy. A weaker euro adds to it.

euro_area_unemployment_rate.what: the share of people in the euro area who want a job and are looking, but do not have one (EU-standard definition).
euro_area_unemployment_rate.why: the ECB calls the labour market “robust”. Low unemployment means the economy can cope with higher rates, but it can also keep wages, and service prices, rising.

german_registered_unemployment_nationa.what: people registered as unemployed at German job centres. Germany's national count is broader than the EU-standard measure, so the rate is higher.
german_registered_unemployment_nationa.why: this is the number most Germans hear on the news. It is slowly rising. BA head Andrea Nahles said: “Im September beginnt am Arbeitsmarkt die Herbstbelebung. Der Auftakt fällt allerdings schwunglos aus.” (In our words: the usual autumn pick-up has started, but without momentum.)

german_unemployment_rate_eu_standard_i.what: Germany's unemployment measured the same way as other EU countries, from a household survey.
german_unemployment_rate_eu_standard_i.why: it lets you compare Germany with the euro-area average (6.4%). Germany is still low, but higher than a year ago.

people_in_work_in_germany.what: everyone living in Germany who has a job, including the self-employed.
people_in_work_in_germany.why: employment has been falling on average every month this year. It is the clearest sign of weakness in Germany's economy.

german_underemployment.what: the unemployed plus people in job schemes or training who would otherwise be unemployed.
german_underemployment.why: a fuller picture of slack in the jobs market. It edged down last month.

short_time_work_kurzarbeit.what: workers on reduced hours with part of their lost pay covered by the state, instead of being laid off.
short_time_work_kurzarbeit.why: it rises fast when firms are in trouble. It is falling, a sign companies are not in crisis.

job_vacancies_registered_in_germany.what: open jobs that companies reported to the employment agency.
job_vacancies_registered_in_germany.why: more vacancies than a year ago is a small positive sign of demand for workers.

euro_area_pay_growth_compensation_per.what: average pay per worker across the euro area. The ECB's wage tracker points to negotiated wage growth of 2.7% in the first half of 2027.
euro_area_pay_growth_compensation_per.why: pay is not speeding up despite higher prices. That is the main reason officials say there are no clear signs yet of a wage-price spiral.

german_gdp_growth.what: GDP (gross domestic product) is the total value of everything Germany produces, after removing price rises. +0.3% is growth over one quarter (roughly 1.2% at a yearly pace); output was 1.0% higher than a year earlier.
german_gdp_growth.why: growth came mainly from exports (+2.0%); household spending rose only 0.1% and investment fell 0.2%. We mark it “Old” because it covers spring.

euro_area_gdp_growth.what: the same measure for the whole euro area; +1.2% on a year earlier.
euro_area_gdp_growth.why: the euro area grew twice as fast as Germany in spring. The ECB said growth was spread across countries and sectors, which gives it room to raise rates.

ifo_business_climate_germany.what: a monthly survey of German companies about their business now and over the next six months.
ifo_business_climate_germany.why: it rose for the second month in a row despite high energy prices. But retailers remain very cautious because of rising inflation. The October reading comes on Oct 26, before the meeting.

german_industrial_production.what: how much German factories, builders and energy firms produced.
german_industrial_production.why: a good August, driven by construction and machinery. But energy-intensive industries (chemicals, metals) fell again, showing the cost of expensive energy.

german_factory_orders.what: new orders received by German manufacturers.
german_factory_orders.why: the drop looks alarming but was almost entirely due to fewer giant orders for ships, trains and aircraft after an unusually big July. Without large orders, orders were nearly flat (−0.1%).

german_exports.what: the value of goods Germany sold abroad.
german_exports.why: exports drove Germany's spring growth. A small dip is not alarming, but ifo reports export expectations fell in September.

ecb_staff_growth_forecast_euro_area.what: what ECB economists expect for euro-area growth: 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027, 1.5% in 2028.
ecb_staff_growth_forecast_euro_area.why: growth forecasts were revised up because the economy proved resilient. The ECB still sees growth risks “to the downside”.

german_growth_forecast_joint_economic.what: the joint forecast of Germany's leading economic research institutes. It expects 1.1% growth next year.
german_growth_forecast_joint_economic.why: Germany is recovering, helped by government spending, but the institutes say the recovery “rests on a narrow foundation”. Nagel said growth of “around 1 %” is possible this year.

ecb_deposit_facility_rate_the_main_pol.what: the interest banks earn on money they park overnight at the central bank. Because banks have plenty of spare cash, this is the rate that steers all others.
ecb_deposit_facility_rate_the_main_pol.why: this is the ECB's main “pedal”. The October 29 decision is about keeping it at 2.50%, raising it to 2.75%, or lowering it.

ecb_main_refinancing_rate.what: the rate banks pay to borrow from the ECB for a week. The marginal lending rate (overnight emergency borrowing) is 2.90%.
ecb_main_refinancing_rate.why: all three ECB rates move together, so you can follow just the deposit rate.

2_year_german_government_bond_schatz.what: the yield on the federal note maturing in September 2028.
2_year_german_government_bond_schatz.why: this rate mostly reflects what investors expect the ECB to do over the next two years. At 3.07%, well above the 2.50% ECB rate, it tells us markets expect further rises.

10_year_german_government_bond_bund.what: the yield on the Bund maturing in August 2036, Europe's benchmark long-term interest rate. The monthly average was 3.18% in August (OECD via FRED).
10_year_german_government_bond_bund.why: German fixed-rate mortgages follow this rate. Its rise makes buying homes and investing more expensive, which slows the economy on its own. Lane said the ECB is “studying this trend in the financial data very closely.”

30_year_german_government_bond.what: the yield on the Bund maturing in 2056.
30_year_german_government_bond.why: it shows the long-term cost of government borrowing, which matters for Germany's growing defence and infrastructure spending. It was steady in early October.

market_expectations_for_ecb_rates.what: the ECB's own summary of what financial markets were pricing in: “a further two to three hikes priced in by the end of 2027.” Surveyed analysts were calmer and expected the rate to “plateau at 2.50%”.
market_expectations_for_ecb_rates.why: markets expect more rises over time, but this says nothing about October alone. We mark it “Secondary” because we did not see the raw market data ourselves, and it is a month old.

bank_lending_rates_for_firms_and_homes.what: the average rates banks charged on new business loans and mortgages. Loans to firms grew 4.4% in July; mortgage lending growth eased to 3.0%.
bank_lending_rates_for_firms_and_homes.why: lending is still growing, so higher rates have not choked off credit. These figures predate the September rise.

euro_vs_u_s_dollar.what: how many U.S. dollars one euro buys, as fixed daily by the ECB. The low for the period shown was $1.1177 on October 7.
euro_vs_u_s_dollar.why: oil is priced in dollars. A weaker euro makes energy and other imports dearer for Germans, adding to inflation. It is one reason the ECB could lean toward raising.

oil_price_brent_crude_european_benchma.what: the price of a barrel of North Sea crude oil, the benchmark for Europe.
oil_price_brent_crude_european_benchma.why: Brent swung by $20 within a week. Oil above $120 keeps fuel and heating oil, and therefore inflation, high. It is far above the U.S. WTI price; our reading is that supply to Europe is tighter than to the U.S.

oil_price_wti_crude_u_s.why: shown for comparison with our U.S. page. Europe pays the Brent price, which is much higher.

natural_gas_price_europe.what: the average price of natural gas in Europe, in U.S. dollars.
natural_gas_price_europe.why: gas heats German homes and powers industry. Nagel warned gas is “especially vulnerable because storage levels are low”. We mark it “Old” because the latest figure is for July.

german_fuel_tax_cut_tankrabatt.what: a German government tax cut on fuel. ifo found stations passed on about 15 of 17 cents for diesel in the first five days.
german_fuel_tax_cut_tankrabatt.why: it should lower German fuel prices and German inflation in October. But it does not lower world oil prices, and it is a German measure, so its effect on euro-area inflation is limited.

u_s_federal_reserve_rate.what: the main U.S. interest rate. The Fed also raised in September because of the same energy shock.
u_s_federal_reserve_rate.why: U.S. rates are much higher than the ECB's 2.50%, which helps explain why the dollar is strong and the euro weak. The Fed decides on October 28, one day before the ECB.

w: What it said: inflation is expected to stay “well above target for an extended period”, the ECB will act meeting by meeting and is “not pre-committing to a particular rate path.” Lagarde: “We are not taking a view as to which direction we go at our next meeting.”
Why it matters: the ECB deliberately keeps October open. Unlike the Fed, it gives no chart of officials' expected rates.

said.n: Account of the September meeting (detailed notes)
w: What it said: “Members largely agreed that the inflation outlook had deteriorated.” Lane called the rise to 2.50% “a robust decision”. Some members held the view “that the adverse scenario was more likely than the baseline.” But “So far, indirect effects remained contained, with no material signs of second-round effects.”
Why it matters: it shows real concern, but no sign of a plan to act at the very next meeting.

said.v: “we are not on a pre-committed rate path”
w: What he said: “It was prudent to raise the policy rate from 2.00 to 2.50 per cent”; the ECB remains in the “middle path”; a new wave of the energy shock “poses direct upside risks to the inflation outlook”.
Why it matters: Lane prepares the policy proposal at each meeting. He sees upside risks but gave no signal that October is the moment.

said.v: “energy prices are higher than we expected in our baseline.”
w: What he said: “When inflation is too high, the policy rate has to go up.” But higher long-term rates “slows down the European economy and, on its own, reduces the inflation rate.”
Why it matters: he points to both the problem (energy above forecast) and a reason to wait (the bond market is already tightening).

said.v: “This may lead us to raise rates…”
w: What she said: “This may lead us to raise rates, at the risk of weighing on the financing of the economy and consequently on growth.” Earlier (Sep 12) she said “we are obliged to react” to a shock that is “longer-lasting”.
Why it matters: she leaves the door open to more rises but stresses the cost to growth. No timing given.

said.v: “We had two rate increases at projection meetings.”
w: What he said: “We will see what happens in the coming months and adjust policy accordingly.” He added: “The expectation now is that energy prices will stay elevated for longer.”
Why it matters: the link between rate moves and forecast meetings is one of the main reasons we lean toward December rather than October.

What he said: “We have therefore responded cautiously, but firmly.” “However, this does not mean that monetary policy can simply ignore the energy price shock.” But “there are so far no clear signs that inflation has fed through to price and wage setting.”
Why it matters: Nagel is Germany's representative on the ECB Council. He supports the rises but did not call for one in October.

said.n: Clemens Fuest, ifo Institute (not an ECB official)
said.v: Rise “comes at an inopportune time for Germany”
w: What he said: “Given that the economy remains quite weak despite some rays of hope, the interest rate hike comes at an inopportune time for Germany,” adding: “However, the ECB has a mandate to conduct monetary policy for the entire eurozone.”
Why it matters: it captures the German dilemma. The ECB's rate fits the euro-area average, not Germany alone.

gaps: Final September euro-area inflation comes out on October 16, two days after this page. Why it matters: it is the most important report before the meeting, so our view may be out of date by Friday.

Market odds for October alone. We found no official source. The ECB's meeting account says markets priced “a further two to three hikes” by end-2027 at the time of the September meeting, but gives no October number. Why it matters: we cannot compare our 37% chance of an October rise with what markets expect today.

Bund yields after October 8. The Bundesbank's daily time series did not load for us, so our latest bond rates are from its October 8 price list. Why it matters: a big move since then would change one of our arguments for Hold.

The full decision section of the September meeting account could not be read (the page was cut off for us), so we rely on Lagarde's statement that the decision was unanimous and do not know how many members argued for a bigger or faster move.

Whether Nagel votes in October. ECB voting rights rotate among national central bank heads, so not every governor votes at every meeting. We did not check the rotation for October. Why it matters: little in practice, because all Council members take part in the discussion.

Release dates for the October flash inflation figures (euro area and Germany), the third-quarter GDP estimates and the ECB's October Bank Lending Survey could not be confirmed on official calendars. Why it matters: if German October prices (lowered by the fuel tax cut) come out before October 29, they could make waiting easier.
Isabel Schnabel's recent views and speeches by other euro-area governors were not collected; for Schnabel we found only presentation slides without text.
Daily European gas prices (TTF) were not collected; the gas price shown is a July monthly average. The duration and cost of Germany's fuel tax cut were not confirmed.
ifo forecast discrepancy. ifo's September 3 headline cites 1.4% German growth for 2026, but the page summary we read mentions 0.8%; we did not resolve this and do not use either figure.

How we gathered data: a web search tool was not available for this build. Every number was read directly from the official page linked next to it, through a page-reading tool that returns extracts; quotes are short passages that tool reported word-for-word.

group_intros.prices: These numbers tell us how fast things are getting more expensive. The ECB's goal is about 2% a year for the whole euro area, measured by HICP. German figures are shown too: they matter to people in Germany, but the ECB's target is the euro-area average.
group_intros.jobs: These numbers show whether people can find and keep work. The ECB's legal target is prices, not jobs, but a weak jobs market makes it more careful about raising rates.
group_intros.growth: These numbers show how fast the economy is growing. A strong economy can handle higher interest rates; a weak one cannot. Germany is the euro area's biggest economy, but the ECB looks at the whole area.
group_intros.rates: These numbers show the ECB's own rates and the rates set by investors in financial markets. German government bonds (“Bunds”) are the euro area's benchmark, and German mortgages follow them closely.
group_intros.said: ECB officials often hint at what they will do next. Reading their words carefully is one of the best ways to guess the next decision. Quotes are short extracts from the official pages linked.
group_intros.global: Germany and the euro area import most of their energy, so world energy prices and what other central banks do matter a lot.

copy.story_intro: This is the story of the past year, in order. Each step explains what happened, why it happened, and what it meant for ordinary people in Germany. The line at the bottom of each step (“Because of this…”) shows how it led to the next step, so you can follow cause and effect from start to finish.
copy.choices_intro: At every meeting the ECB has three options. Below we explain what each one would mean, why it could happen, why it might not, and what it would mean in everyday life. Analysis · our judgement
copy.report_intro: Think of this as a school report for the economy in four subjects. Green means healthy. Yellow means mixed, keep watching. Red means a problem the central bank must fix. Each grade is also written in words, so you do not need to see the color. Analysis
copy.gaps_intro: Good research is honest about its blind spots. Here is what is missing, delayed or unverified, and why it matters.
copy.numbers_intro: Every number we used, grouped by topic. For each one you will see the latest value, the period it covers, when it was published, the previous value, where it came from, and, most importantly, a plain explanation of what it is and why it matters. Tap a group to open or close it. Observed facts

live_before.html: The numbers on this page are a snapshot taken on October 14, 2026. If you want to see whether anything has changed since then, you can try loading the newest values from FRED, a free public data service run by the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis that also carries European data. Note: the FRED euro-area series shown here cover 19 countries, so they can differ slightly from the 21-country figures above, and some German series arrive later than the official German releases.

How it works: FRED gives anyone a free “API key”, a code that works like a library card for its data. Paste your key below and press Refresh. The newest values appear in a separate table, next to our snapshot values so you can compare. The rest of this page stays exactly as it is.
Privacy: your key is saved only in this browser, on this device, and is sent only to FRED. Press “Forget key” to remove it. Get a free key at fred.stlouisfed.org.

live_after.html: Good to know: FRED often does not allow web pages to request its data directly, so many browsers will block this. If that happens, you will see a clear message and nothing on the page will change. You can always check the same numbers yourself on the FRED website.
